Twice-punctured hyperbolic sphere with a conical singularity and generalized elliptic integral

G. D. Anderson, T. Sugawa, M. K. Vamanamurthy, and M. Vuorinen
Abstract.

We describe, in terms of generalized elliptic integrals, the hyperbolic metric of the twice-punctured sphere with one conical singularity of prescribed order. We also give several monotonicity properties of the metric and a couple of applications.

Key words and phrases: 
Hypergeometric functions, generalized complete elliptic integrals, conformal mapping
2000 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 30F45, secondary 30C80, 33C75.

1. Introduction

The hyperbolic metric ρ⁡(z)​|d​z|\rho(z)|dz| on the thrice-punctured sphere ℂ^∖{0,1,∞}{\widehat{\mathbb{C}}}\setminus\{0,1,\infty\} is one of the fundamental tools in complex analysis. Indeed, for instance, the big Picard theorem can be derived by a careful look at the metric ρ⁡(z)​|d​z|\rho(z)|dz| and the distance induced by it. It is known that the density function ρ⁡(z)\rho(z) can be expressed explicitly as

ρ⁡(z)=π8​|z⁡(1−z)|​Re⁡{K⁡(z)​K​(1−z¯)},\rho(z)=\frac{\pi}{8|z(1-z)|{\,\operatorname{Re}\,}\{{\mathrm{K}}(z){\mathrm{K}}(1-\bar{z})\}},

where K⁡(z){\mathrm{K}}(z) is the complete elliptic integral of the first kind given in (3.1) (see [2] or [15]). On the other hand, it has been recognized that generalized elliptic integrals Ka​(z){\mathrm{K}}_{a}(z) and Ea​(z),{\mathrm{E}}_{a}(z), defined in (3.2) and (3.3) respectively, share many properties with the original complete elliptic integrals (cf. [4]).

In the present paper, it is shown that the hyperbolic metric of a twice-punctured sphere with one conical singularity of prescribed angle can be expressed in terms of these generalized complete elliptic integrals.

2. Hyperbolic metric with conical singularities

A hyperbolic metric of a compact Riemann surface RR with conical singularities of angle 2πθj,θj∈[0,+∞)∖{1},2\pi\theta_{j},~\theta_{j}\in[0,+\infty)\setminus\{1\}, at points pj∈R,j=1,…,N,p_{j}\in R,~j=1,\dots,N, is a conformal metric on R∖{p1,…,pN}R\setminus\{p_{1},\dots,p_{N}\} of the form d​s=eφ⁡(z)​|d​z|,ds=e^{\varphi(z)}|dz|, where φ\varphi is a smooth function satisfying the Liouville equation

(2.1) Δ​φ=4​e2​φ\varDelta\varphi=4e^{2\varphi}

on R∖{p1,…,pN}R\setminus\{p_{1},\dots,p_{N}\} and possessing the asymptotic behavior

(2.2) φ⁡(z)={−(1−θj)​log⁡|z−zj|+O⁡(1)if​θj>0,−log⁡|z−zj|−log⁡(−log⁡|z−zj|)+O⁡(1)if​θj=0\varphi(z)=\begin{cases}-(1-\theta_{j})\log|z-z_{j}|+O(1)&\quad\text{if}~\theta_{j}>0,\\ -\log|z-z_{j}|-\log(-\log|z-z_{j}|)+O(1)&\quad\text{if}~\theta_{j}=0\end{cases}

as z→zj=z⁡(pj),z\to z_{j}=z(p_{j}), where zz is a local coordinate of RR around pj.p_{j}. Note that a conical singularity of angle 00 is called a puncture or a cusp.

The remainder term O⁡(1)O(1) in the above is known to be continuous at z=zjz=z_{j} by a detailed study of the local behavior of solutions to the Liouville equation at the isolated singularities by Nitsche [12] (see also [9]).

Heins [8, Chap. II] proved that for a compact Riemann surface RR of genus gg and finite points in it with given angles as above, a hyperbolic metric on RR with the behavior described in (2.2) exists uniquely as long as the condition

(2.3) 2​(1−g)−∑j=1N(1−θj)<02(1-g)-\sum_{j=1}^{N}(1-\theta_{j})<0

is satisfied. This constraint comes from the Gauss-Bonnet formula. This result was previously known by Picard [13] when g=0.g=0. Practically, this unique metric as above is called the (complete) hyperbolic metric of the Riemann surface R∖{p1,…,pn}R\setminus\{p_{1},\dots,p_{n}\} with conical singularities of angle 2​π​θj2\pi\theta_{j} at pj​(j=n+1,…,N),p_{j}~(j=n+1,\dots,N), where θ1=⋯=θn=0<θj≠1​(j=n+1,…,N).\theta_{1}=\dots=\theta_{n}=0<\theta_{j}\neq 1~(j=n+1,\dots,N).

The hyperbolic metric treated in the present paper corresponds to the case when R=ℂ^,g=0,N=3,(p1,p2,p3)=(0,1,∞)R={\widehat{\mathbb{C}}},~g=0,~N=3,~(p_{1},p_{2},p_{3})=(0,1,\infty) and (θ1,θ2,θ3)=(0,0,2​π​α),(\theta_{1},\theta_{2},\theta_{3})=(0,0,2\pi\alpha), where 0≤α<1.0\leq\alpha<1. Note here that this case always satisfies the condition (2.3). We denote this metric by ρα​(z)​|d​z|.\rho_{\alpha}(z)|dz|.

When α=0,\alpha=0, the metric ρ0\rho_{0} is simply the usual hyperbolic metric ρ\rho of ℂ^∖{0,1,∞}=ℂ∖{0,1}{\widehat{\mathbb{C}}}\setminus\{0,1,\infty\}=\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0,1\} (without conical singularities). By uniqueness of the hyperbolic metric with conical singularities, the metric admits the obvious symmetry ρα​(z)=ρα​(1−z)=ρα​(z¯).\rho_{\alpha}(z)=\rho_{\alpha}(1-z)=\rho_{\alpha}(\bar{z}).

We remark that for a Möbius transformation M,M, ρα​(M⁡(z))​|M′​(z)|\rho_{\alpha}(M(z))|M^{\prime}(z)| gives the density of the hyperbolic metric of ℂ^∖{M⁡(0),M⁡(1)}{\widehat{\mathbb{C}}}\setminus\{M(0),M(1)\} with a conical singularity of angle 2​π​α2\pi\alpha at M⁡(∞).M(\infty). For instance, the hyperbolic metric ρ~α​(z)​|d​z|\tilde{\rho}_{\alpha}(z)|dz| of the twice-punctured sphere ℂ^∖{1,∞}=ℂ∖{1}{\widehat{\mathbb{C}}}\setminus\{1,\infty\}=\mathbb{C}\setminus\{1\} with a conical singularity of angle 2​π​α2\pi\alpha at 00 can be obtained by ρ~α​(z)=ρα​(1/z)/|z|2.\tilde{\rho}_{\alpha}(z)=\rho_{\alpha}(1/z)/|z|^{2}.

(3.2) Ka​(z)\displaystyle{\mathrm{K}}_{a}(z) =π2​F​(a,1−a,1,z)\displaystyle=\frac{\pi}{2}F(a,1-a;1;z)
=sin⁡(π​a)​∫01t1−2​a​d​t(1−t2)1−a​(1−z​t2)a\displaystyle=\sin(\pi a)\int_{0}^{1}\frac{t^{1-2a}dt}{(1-t^{2})^{1-a}(1-z\,t^{2})^{a}}

We remark that the above definition is slightly different from the usual one. The (traditional) generalized complete elliptic integrals of the first and the second kind usually refer to Ka​(x2){\mathrm{K}}_{a}(x^{2}) and Ea​(x2){\mathrm{E}}_{a}(x^{2}) for 0<x<10<x<1 in our notation.

We mean by Ka′{\mathrm{K}}_{a}^{\prime} and Ea′{\mathrm{E}}_{a}^{\prime} the derivatives of Ka{\mathrm{K}}_{a} and Ea,{\mathrm{E}}_{a}, though these are often used to mean the complementary functions. (3.4) Ka∗​(z)​Ea​(z)+Ea∗​(z)​Ka​(z)−Ka∗​(z)​Ka​(z)=π​sin⁡(π​a)4​(1−a).{\mathrm{K}}_{a}^{*}(z){\mathrm{E}}_{a}(z)+{\mathrm{E}}_{a}^{*}(z){\mathrm{K}}_{a}(z)-{\mathrm{K}}_{a}^{*}(z){\mathrm{K}}_{a}(z)=\frac{\pi\sin(\pi a)}{4(1-a)}.

4. Computation of ρα​(z)\rho_{\alpha}(z)

A relation between conformal mappings and the generalized complete elliptic integral Ka​(z){\mathrm{K}}_{a}(z) of the first kind is given by [4, Theorem 2.2] when the argument zz is real and between 00 and 1.1. We will now give another aspect of Ka​(z){\mathrm{K}}_{a}(z) for the complex argument z.z.

As is stated in [16, Lemma 2], the hyperbolic metric of the sphere with given conical singularities can be described in terms of solutions to a second-order Fuchsian differential equation with regular singularities at the cone points. In our case, the metric is described explicitly in terms of generalized elliptic integrals.

We begin with a general case. Let aa, bb, and cc be real numbers. It is a classical fact that the function f⁡(z)=i​F​(a,b,a+b+1−c,1−z)/F⁡(a,b,c,z)f(z)=i\,F(a,b;a+b+1-c;1-z)/F(a,b;c;z) maps the upper half plane ℍ\mathbb{H} onto a curvilinear triangle bounded by three circular arcs and having the interior angles (1−c)​π(1-c)\pi at f⁡(0),(c−a−b)​πf(0),~(c-a-b)\pi at f⁡(1),f(1), and (b−a)​π(b-a)\pi at f⁡(∞),f(\infty), provided that these angles are all nonnegative and the sum is less than π\pi (see, for instance, [11, pp. 206, 207]). Note that the segment (0,1)(0,1) of the real axis is mapped by ff to a part of the imaginary axis and that ff maps ℂ∖((−∞,0]∪[1,+∞))\mathbb{C}\setminus((-\infty,0]\cup[1,+\infty)) conformally onto the domain which is the union of f⁡((,,,)),f((0,1)), f⁡(ℍ)f(\mathbb{H}), and its reflection in the imaginary axis.

In the particular case when 0<a<1,b=1−a0<a<1,~b=1-a, and c=1,c=1, the function ff can be written in the form i​Ka​(1−z)/Ka​(z)i\,{\mathrm{K}}_{a}(1-z)/{\mathrm{K}}_{a}(z), and the image f⁡(ℍ)f(\mathbb{H}) is a circular triangle with interior angles 00, 00, and |1−2​a|​π.|1-2a|\pi. More specifically, we have the following result.

4.1 Lemma.

Let fa​(z)=i​Ka​(1−z)/Ka​(z),0<a<1.f_{a}(z)=i\,{\mathrm{K}}_{a}(1-z)/{\mathrm{K}}_{a}(z),~0<a<1. Then the image fa​(ℍ)f_{a}(\mathbb{H}) of the upper half plane ℍ\mathbb{H} under faf_{a} is the hyperbolic triangle Δa\Delta_{a} in ℍ\mathbb{H} whose interior angles are 00, 00, and |1−2​a|​π|1-2a|\pi at the vertices 00, ∞\infty, and e|1−2​a|​π​i/2,e^{|1-2a|\pi i/2}, respectively. More precisely, Δa={w∈ℍ: 0<Re⁡w⁡<sin⁡(π​a),|2​w​sin⁡(π​a)−1|>​1}.\Delta_{a}=\{w\in\mathbb{H}:\ 0<{\,\operatorname{Re}\,}w<\sin(\pi a),~|2w\sin(\pi a)-1|>1\}.

Proof.

Since fa​(ℍ)f_{a}(\mathbb{H}) is a Jordan domain, faf_{a} extends to a homeomorphism from the closure of ℍ\mathbb{H} onto the closure of fa​(ℍ).f_{a}(\mathbb{H}). First note that faf_{a} maps the interval (0,1)(0,1) onto the whole positive imaginary axis. Since the interior angles of fa​(ℍ)f_{a}(\mathbb{H}) at fa​(0)f_{a}(0) and fa​(1)f_{a}(1) are both 0,0, the boundary arcs fa​((,,,))f_{a}((1,+\infty)) and fa​((,,,))f_{a}((-\infty,0)) are contained in hyperbolic geodesics in ℍ\mathbb{H} of the forms |w−r|=r⁡(0<r)|w-r|=r~(0<r) and Re⁡w=p⁡(p>0),{\,\operatorname{Re}\,}w=p~(p>0), respectively. Since we know that these two geodesics form an angle of θ=|1−2​a|​π,\theta=|1-2a|\pi, we find that r⁡(1+cos⁡θ)=pr(1+\cos\theta)=p by elementary geometry. Thus, it is enough to show that p=sin⁡(π​a),p=\sin(\pi a), which leads to the relation r=sin⁡(π​a)/(1+cos⁡((1−2​a)​π))=1/(2​sin⁡(π​a)).r=\sin(\pi a)/(1+\cos((1-2a)\pi))=1/(2\sin(\pi a)).

Since faf_{a} maps each of the intervals (−∞,0)(-\infty,0),  (0,1)(0,1), and (1,+∞)(1,+\infty) onto a hyperbolic geodesic segment in ℍ,\mathbb{H}, the pull-back fa∗​ρℍ=ρℍ​(fa​(z))​|fa′​(z)|​|d​z|f_{a}^{*}\rho_{\mathbb{H}}=\rho_{\mathbb{H}}(f_{a}(z))|f_{a}^{\prime}(z)||dz| of the hyperbolic (or Poincaré) metric ρℍ​(z)​|d​z|=|d​z|\rho_{\mathbb{H}}(z)|dz|=|dz| /(2​Im⁡(z))/(2{\,\operatorname{Im}\,}(z)) of the upper half plane ℍ\mathbb{H}, together with its reflection fa∗​ρℍ​(z¯)​|d​z|f_{a}^{*}\rho_{\mathbb{H}}(\bar{z})|dz| defines a smooth conformal metric on ℂ∖{0,1}.\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0,1\}. Agard [2] gave a formula for ρℂ∖{0,1}=ρ0\rho_{\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0,1\}}=\rho_{0} in terms of complete elliptic integrals. In the same way, we can compute ρα\rho_{\alpha} for 0≤α<10\leq\alpha<1 with the help of the above construction.

4.7 Theorem.

Let 0≤α<10\leq\alpha<1 and choose 0<a<10<a<1 so that α=|1−2​a|.\alpha=|1-2a|. The hyperbolic metric ρα​(z)​|d​z|\rho_{\alpha}(z)|dz| of the twice-punctured sphere ℂ^∖{0,1}{\widehat{\mathbb{C}}}\setminus\{0,1\} with conical singularity of angle 2​π​α2\pi\alpha at ∞\infty is given by

(4.8) ρα​(z)=π​cos⁡(π​α/2)8​|z⁡(1−z)|​Re⁡(Ka​(z)​Ka​(1−z¯)).\rho_{\alpha}(z)=\frac{\pi\cos(\pi\alpha/2)}{8|z(1-z)|{\,\operatorname{Re}\,}\big({\mathrm{K}}_{a}(z){\mathrm{K}}_{a}(1-\bar{z})\big)}.
Proof.

By Gauss’ contiguous relations (see (2.5.8) of [5]), one obtains

z⁡(1−z)​Ka′​(z)=(1−a)​[Ea​(z)−(1−z)​Ka​(z)].z(1-z){\mathrm{K}}_{a}^{\prime}(z)=(1-a)\big[{\mathrm{E}}_{a}(z)-(1-z){\mathrm{K}}_{a}(z)\big].

Using this identity, we derive

=−i1−az⁡(1−z)⋅Ea∗​(z)​Ka​(z)+Ka∗​(z)​Ea​(z)−Ka∗​(z)​Ka​(z)(Ka​(z))2\displaystyle=-i\,\frac{1-a}{z(1-z)}\cdot\frac{{\mathrm{E}}_{a}^{*}(z){\mathrm{K}}_{a}(z)+{\mathrm{K}}_{a}^{*}(z){\mathrm{E}}_{a}(z)-{\mathrm{K}}_{a}^{*}(z){\mathrm{K}}_{a}(z)}{({\mathrm{K}}_{a}(z))^{2}}
=−i​π​sin⁡(π​a)4​z​(1−z)​(Ka​(z))2,\displaystyle=-i\,\frac{\pi\sin(\pi a)}{4z(1-z)({\mathrm{K}}_{a}(z))^{2}},

where we have used (3.4). Hence, using the relation Ka​(z)¯=Ka​(z¯),\overline{{\mathrm{K}}_{a}(z)}={\mathrm{K}}_{a}(\bar{z}), we obtain

5. Applications

We conclude the present note with a few applications of our metric ρα.\rho_{\alpha}. Since no concrete estimates for ρα\rho_{\alpha} are given so far, we will give only general principles to refine classical results.

If a meromorphic function ff on the unit disk 𝔻{\mathbb{D}} does not assume the three points 0,10,1 and ∞,\infty, then the principle of hyperbolic metric gives us the inequality f∗​ρ≤ρ𝔻,f^{*}\rho\leq\rho_{\mathbb{D}}, namely;

ρ⁡(f⁡(z))​|f′​(z)|≤11−|z|2,z∈𝔻.\rho(f(z))|f^{\prime}(z)|\leq\frac{1}{1-|z|^{2}},\quad z\in{\mathbb{D}}.

The classical theorems of Picard and Schottky follow essentially from the above inequality (see, for example, [3, §1-9]). We can now relax the assumption about the omitted values as in the following.

5.1 Theorem.

Let ff be a meromorphic function on the unit disk omitting the two values 00 and 1.1. Suppose that every pole of ff is of order at least k≥2.k\geq 2. Then the following inequality holds:

ρ1/k​(f⁡(z))​|f′​(z)|≤11−|z|2,z∈𝔻.\rho_{1/k}(f(z))|f^{\prime}(z)|\leq\frac{1}{1-|z|^{2}},\quad z\in{\mathbb{D}}.
Proof.

Let α>1/k.\alpha>1/k. We may assume that ff is not constant. Let λ\lambda be the pull-back metric f∗​ραf^{*}\rho_{\alpha} of ρα\rho_{\alpha} under f.f. Then it is easily verified that the Gaussian curvature of λ\lambda is −4-4 off the set of poles and branch points of f.f. Let z0z_{0} be a pole of f.f. Then the order mm of the pole at z0z_{0} is at least kk by assumption. In view of (3.5), we have

=[(1+α)​m−(m+1)]​log⁡|z−z0|+O⁡(1)\displaystyle=\big[(1+\alpha)m-(m+1)\big]\log|z-z_{0}|+O(1)
=(α​m−1)​log⁡|z−z0|+O⁡(1)\displaystyle=\left(\alpha m-1\right)\log|z-z_{0}|+O(1)

as z→z0.z\to z_{0}. Since α​m>1,\alpha m>1, we see that λ⁡(z0)=0.\lambda(z_{0})=0. Thus λ\lambda is an ultrahyperbolic metric on 𝔻{\mathbb{D}} in the sense of Ahlfors [3]. Thus, Ahlfors’ lemma now yields f∗​ρα≤ρ𝔻.f^{*}\rho_{\alpha}\leq\rho_{\mathbb{D}}. Taking the limit as α→1/k,\alpha\to 1/k, we obtain the required inequality. ∎

Knowledge about the hyperbolic metric ρ=ρ0\rho=\rho_{0} of the thrice-punctured sphere ℂ∖{0,1}\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0,1\} has led to various useful estimates for the hyperbolic metric of a general plane domain (see, for instance, [6] or [15]). We now use ρα\rho_{\alpha} instead of ρ0\rho_{0} to obtain similar estimates for the hyperbolic metric with conical singularities.

5.2 Theorem.

Otherwise, by the local behavior of solutions to the Liouville equation around an isolated singularity due to Nitsche [12], we see that vv can be extended continuously to the point wj.w_{j}. Recall now the following fact: Suppose that uu is a continuous function on an open neighborhood DD of a point aa and subharmonic on D∖{a}.D\setminus\{a\}. Then uu is subharmonic on D.D. Thus vv is subharmonic on Ω′=Ω∪{wj:wj​is isolated}\Omega^{\prime}=\Omega\cup\{w_{j}:w_{j}~\text{is isolated}\} and vanishes in a neighborhood of ∂Ω′∪S.\partial\Omega^{\prime}\cup S. We now appeal to the maximum principle to conclude that v=0v=0 in Ω,\Omega, which means μ≤λ.\mu\leq\lambda. The proof is now complete. ∎
